questions.hintStrategy: For older-adult SATA items, reject options based on age stereotypes; select those based on the client’s actual needs.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old needs a throat swab in the clinic. Which approaches by the nurse are developmentally appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Offer a limited choice, such as “Red sticker or blue sticker after?”
Tell the child, “This won’t feel like anything at all.”
Say, “Big kids don’t cry,” if the child begins to cry.
Give one short direction at a time, such as “Open wide like a lion.”
Let the child sit on the caregiver’s lap during the swab.
Explain in detail why the swab is needed before starting.
optionRationales: Correct. Limited safe choices give some control.
Incorrect. Dishonest statements damage trust.
Incorrect. This judges the child’s feelings.
Correct. One concrete step at a time fits a toddler’s language.
Correct. Caregiver support comforts a young child.
Incorrect. Long explanations exceed a toddler’s attention and language.
questions.rationale: Toddlers and young preschoolers need short, concrete words, one-step directions, familiar comfort, and limited safe choices. A caregiver’s lap gives security, and a simple choice offers a sense of control. Detailed explanations are tempting because honesty is important, but the child cannot process them, so a brief honest statement works better. Promising no sensation and shaming the child for crying both undermine trust.
questions.takeaway: Young children need one concrete step, caregiver support, and limited choices.
questions.hintContent: Think about attention span and language at age 3.
questions.hintStrategy: For pediatric SATA items, check each option against the child’s developmental stage.

questions.stem: A nurse is interviewing a 15-year-old client about risk behaviors at a well visit. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the parent the risk questions to save time.
Ask the parent to step out for part of the visit.
Explain which information may need to be shared and why.
Promise that nothing the teen says will ever be shared.
Listen without showing shock when the teen discloses vaping.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The teen is the best source and needs to answer directly.
Correct. Private time helps teens share sensitive information.
Correct. Teens need an honest explanation of confidentiality limits.
Incorrect. Total secrecy cannot be promised when safety is at risk.
Correct. Nonjudgmental listening keeps the teen talking.
questions.rationale: Adolescents need private time, nonjudgmental listening, clear expectations, and honest limits of confidentiality. Asking the parent to step out and explaining what may need to be shared builds trust. Promising total secrecy is tempting because it seems to encourage disclosure, but it is dishonest when serious risk may require sharing. Reacting with shock or interviewing the parent instead shuts the teen out.
questions.takeaway: Teens need privacy, honesty about confidentiality limits, and a calm response.
questions.hintContent: What helps a teen speak honestly without a false promise?
questions.hintStrategy: For adolescent SATA items, select privacy and honesty; reject secrecy promises and judgment.

questions.stem: A client has had expressive aphasia since a stroke last year. The client follows directions accurately but struggles to name objects. Which strategies should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
options: Speak louder so the client can process the words.
Offer a picture board or writing pad as appropriate.
Direct questions to the client’s spouse to save effort.
Use simple childlike phrases when speaking to the client.
Ask questions that can be answered with yes or no.
Wait for the client to respond without finishing sentences.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Volume does not address an expressive language problem.
Correct. Alternative methods help the client express needs.
Incorrect. This removes the client’s voice from their own care.
Incorrect. The client understands well; talking down harms dignity.
Correct. Yes/no questions reduce the need for word-finding.
Correct. Allowing time protects the client’s own message.
questions.rationale: Expressive aphasia blocks getting words out, but the client may understand and decide normally. Helpful strategies include yes/no questions, extra time, and alternative methods such as pictures or writing. Speaking louder is tempting because it seems to help any communication problem, but this client’s hearing and understanding are intact. Speaking to the spouse instead or using childlike language both treat the client as less capable than they are.
questions.takeaway: For expressive aphasia, give time and other ways to answer; do not talk down or around the client.
questions.hintContent: What part of communication is actually impaired here?
questions.hintStrategy: In aphasia SATA items, first decide whether the problem is receptive or expressive, then select matching strategies.

questions.stem: A client who is Deaf and uses ASL arrives at the emergency department with abdominal pain. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Request a qualified ASL interpreter in person or by video.
Look at and speak to the client, not the interpreter.
Ask the client’s 10-year-old child to sign questions.
Use good lighting and keep the face visible during talk.
Rely on lip-reading to review the plan of care.
optionRationales: Correct. A qualified interpreter is needed for clinical information.
Correct. Addressing the client keeps the client’s voice central.
Incorrect. Children should not interpret clinical information.
Correct. Visibility supports visual communication.
Incorrect. Lip-reading is unreliable for complex information.
questions.rationale: A Deaf client who uses ASL needs a qualified interpreter for clinical information, delivered in person or by video per policy. The nurse speaks to the client, keeps the face visible in good lighting, and verifies understanding through the interpreter. Using the child is tempting because the child is present and fluent, but it risks errors and burdens the child. Lip-reading misses much of spoken language and is not reliable for clinical decisions.
questions.takeaway: Use a qualified ASL interpreter, face the client, and never rely on a child or lip-reading.
questions.hintContent: Treat ASL as the client’s primary language.
questions.hintStrategy: For language-barrier SATA items, select qualified interpretation and direct address; reject family, children, and shortcuts.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing the communication portion of an admission assessment for a 70-year-old client. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask what has helped the client communicate well in the past.
Assume some hearing loss is present based on the client’s age.
Give a simple request and observe how the client responds.
Rely only on a written checklist to judge comprehension.
Ask the client’s preferred language and communication method.
Ask about usual hearing and vision aids and whether they work.
optionRationales: Correct. The client’s own experience is a resource.
Incorrect. Age alone does not establish a deficit.
Correct. Observing a response helps assess understanding.
Incorrect. Writing may fail because of vision or literacy, not understanding.
Correct. This identifies language needs directly.
Correct. Sensory access must be checked before judging understanding.
questions.rationale: Assessment identifies exactly which part of communication is blocked before choosing a fix. The nurse asks about language, method, hearing, vision, usual aids, and past strategies, then observes a response to a simple request. Assuming hearing loss because of age is tempting because it is common, but it replaces assessment with a stereotype. A written checklist alone can confuse a vision or literacy barrier with poor understanding.
questions.takeaway: Assess language, senses, aids, and response directly; never assume from age.
questions.hintContent: Each correct action gathers data from the client rather than assuming it.
questions.hintStrategy: For assessment SATA items, choose options that collect data; reject options that assume or use a single narrow method.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing the handoff report for a client with expressive aphasia who communicates reliably with a picture board. Which information should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Which needs the client communicates reliably with the board.
How much help the client needs to use the board.
That the client cannot understand, so ask the family instead.
That the client is frustrated and difficult to communicate with.
Where the board is kept and how the client signals yes and no.
optionRationales: Correct. This tells the next nurse what has been verified.
Correct. The level of help keeps the method working.
Incorrect. This is inaccurate; expressive aphasia does not mean poor understanding.
Incorrect. This is a label rather than useful, specific information.
Correct. The next nurse needs the working method right away.
questions.rationale: Once a working communication method is found, it belongs in the record and the handoff so every caregiver can use it. The report should include where the aid is, how yes and no are signaled, which needs are reliably communicated, and how much help is needed. Calling the client “difficult” is tempting because it describes the nurse’s experience, but it is a label that may bias the next caregiver. The client’s ability to understand should not be underestimated.
questions.takeaway: Hand off the working communication method in specific, usable terms.
questions.hintContent: What would the next nurse need to communicate with this client in the first minute?
questions.hintStrategy: For handoff SATA items, choose specific, actionable details and reject labels and assumptions.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: An older adult with moderate hearing loss is in a noisy emergency department hallway bed. The nurse needs to explain the plan for a CT scan. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Shout each word so the client can hear over the noise.
Face the client and speak clearly at a natural pace.
Ask the client to restate the plan in their own words.
Check that the client’s hearing aids are in and working.
Move to a quieter area or reduce nearby noise if possible.
Stand behind the client and speak into the better ear.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Shouting distorts speech and can seem hostile.
Correct. Facing the client allows visual cues.
Correct. Restating checks that the message was received.
Correct. Sensory access must be restored first.
Correct. Background noise blocks hearing.
Incorrect. The client needs to see the speaker’s face.
questions.rationale: For hearing difficulty, the nurse faces the client, reduces noise, checks that hearing aids work, and then confirms understanding by having the client restate the message. Shouting is tempting because the setting is loud, but it distorts sound and may seem angry. Standing behind the client removes facial cues that help with hearing. The check of success is whether the client can restate the message accurately.
questions.takeaway: For hearing loss: aids in, noise down, face the client, then check with restatement.
questions.hintContent: Which actions improve what the client can actually hear and see?
questions.hintStrategy: For sensory-barrier SATA items, select actions that restore access and verify understanding.

questions.stem: At 0845, a nurse documented a 0900 wound dressing change as completed to save time. At 0900, the client declines the dressing change, saying, “Not now, I just got back to sleep.” What should the nurse do?
options: Chart the refusal in a new note and leave the 0900 entry.
Delete the 0900 entry and chart the refusal and plan.
Correct the entry per policy and chart the refusal and plan.
Notify the provider of the refusal and change it later.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Charting the refusal is needed, but the 0900 entry still falsely shows a completed dressing change and must be corrected.
Incorrect. Charting the refusal and plan is right, but deleting the entry hides the error and breaks the audit trail; corrections must stay visible.

Correct. The nurse uses the approved correction process so the original entry stays visible, then documents the refusal, the reason, and the plan. This fixes the false record, which a new note or deletion alone does not.
Incorrect. A refusal may need reporting if it persists, but a single delayed dressing change is not urgent, and the false completed entry would remain.
questions.rationale: Precharting creates a false record because planned care may be delayed, refused, or changed, exactly as happened here. The nurse uses the approved correction process, which keeps the original entry and audit trail visible, and then documents the actual events: the refusal, the client’s stated reason, and the follow-up plan. Deleting the entry is tempting because it seems to clean up the mistake, but hiding an error is never acceptable. Adding a refusal note without correcting the entry leaves conflicting records that could lead another nurse to skip the dressing change.
questions.takeaway: Never prechart; if it happens, correct openly and document what actually occurred.
questions.hintContent: Think about what another nurse would believe after reading the current record.
questions.hintStrategy: For record-error items, choose transparent correction plus accurate documentation; reject options that hide or ignore the error.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse enters a room and finds a 76-year-old client sitting on the floor beside the bed. The client says, “I slipped trying to get to the bathroom.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Document the fall in the client’s record while details are fresh.
Assess the client for injury before moving the client.
Call the client’s family to report the fall.
Help the client back into bed and raise the side rails.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Charting comes after the client is assessed and safe.
Correct. Safety comes first; injuries must be identified before any transfer.
Incorrect. Family notification follows assessment and care.
Incorrect. Moving the client before assessing for injury could worsen harm.
questions.rationale: Charting never comes before safety. When a client falls, the nurse first assesses for injury, then gets help to move the client safely, notifies the provider, and documents promptly and accurately. Documenting right away is tempting because details are fresh, but the record should describe a client who has already been assessed and protected. Moving the client before assessment risks worsening an injury such as a hip fracture.
questions.takeaway: Assess and protect the client first; document promptly afterward.
questions.hintContent: What could go wrong if the nurse skipped straight to the other actions?
questions.hintStrategy: When charting competes with client care in a “first” item, choose the client-care action.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she wrote a client’s blood pressure on the wrong client’s paper flow sheet during a downtime when the EHR was unavailable. Which action is correct?
options: Draw one line through it, keep it readable, and initial it per policy.
Write a note beside it saying it belongs to another client.
Ask the charge nurse to correct the entry on the flow sheet.
Wait and correct the entry once the EHR system is back online.
optionRationales: Correct. One line through the entry keeps it readable, and initials with date and time show who corrected it. This is complete, timely, and done by the nurse who made the error.
Incorrect. Explaining the error is reasonable, but without a line through it the wrong value still looks valid and could be acted on.
Incorrect. Telling the charge nurse may be fine, but the nurse who made the entry is the one who corrects it.
Incorrect. Correcting through the EHR seems tidy, but the paper sheet is the current record, and leaving the error in place risks a wrong decision now.
questions.rationale: Errors must be corrected openly through the approved process, keeping the original entry visible. On paper records, this typically means one line through the entry so it stays readable, a label per policy, and the nurse’s initials with date and time. Writing a note beside the entry is tempting because it explains the mistake, but the wrong value still looks valid. The nurse who made the error corrects it promptly rather than handing it off or waiting for the EHR to return.
questions.takeaway: Correct errors so the original stays visible; never erase, cover, or recopy.
questions.hintContent: Which option leaves an honest trail of both the error and the fix?
questions.hintStrategy: For correction items, choose the option that preserves the original entry.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 1830, a nurse realizes she never documented a dose of as-needed oral pain medication she gave at 1400. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Enter the dose in the 1400 time slot so the record looks complete.
Tell the oncoming nurse the exact dose time during shift report.
Reassess the client’s pain level now and chart that finding.
Make a late entry that shows the current time and the 1400 dose time.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Backdating hides when the entry was really made.
Incorrect. Telling the next nurse helps prevent a repeat dose today, but verbal report is not a permanent record, and the dose still must be charted.
Incorrect. Charting a current pain reassessment is good practice, but it does not record the 1400 dose that was given.
Correct. A labeled late entry is transparent about both times.
questions.rationale: A late entry is clearly labeled and shows when it was written and when the event happened, per policy. This keeps the record accurate and transparent, and it prevents a duplicate dose by the next nurse. Entering it in the 1400 slot is tempting because the dose really was given then, but it hides the delay and misrepresents when documentation occurred. Telling the next nurse in report helps, but only a written entry creates a lasting record.
questions.takeaway: Late entries are labeled and show both the entry time and the event time.
questions.hintContent: What does an honest record of a delayed entry look like?
questions.hintStrategy: For late-documentation items, choose transparency about timing over making the chart look tidy.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse’s neighbor is admitted to another unit of the hospital. The neighbor’s wife texts the nurse, “Can you look up his test results? We haven’t heard anything yet.” Which response is best?
options: “Let me ask a friend who works on his unit to check for you.”
“I’m not on his care team, so I can’t look. His nurse can help.”
“I can look, but only to see if the results are back yet.”
“Ask him to sign a form, and then I can read his chart.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Going to his unit seems proper, but asking a coworker for an informal favor still shares his information without his consent.
Correct. This declines unauthorized access and directs her to the right source.
Incorrect. Even a quick look without a care need is unauthorized access.
Incorrect. A form does not create a care role; access must match the nurse’s job.
questions.rationale: Use the record only for your authorized role and purpose; curiosity or a favor for a friend is not a care need. The nurse declines and points the family to the client’s care team, who can share information according to the client’s wishes. Checking only whether results are back is tempting because it seems harmless, but any access without a role-based need is a breach and shows in the audit trail. Privacy rules apply even when the nurse means well.
questions.takeaway: Access a record only when your role and the client’s care require it.
questions.hintContent: Is the nurse part of this client’s care team?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy items, ask whether access serves an authorized care role; if not, decline and redirect.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 2215, a client with a new urinary tract infection pulls at the IV and says, “Get this off me, there are bugs on it.” The client is oriented to name only; on admission, the client was fully oriented. Which entry is most appropriate?
options: “2215: Client combative and confused; restraints may be needed.”
“2215: Client agitated, likely withdrawal; family should be asked.”
“2215: Pulled at IV, stated ‘there are bugs on it’; oriented to name only.”
“2215: Client had a confused episode but is resting quietly now.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. “Combative” is a label, and the restraint comment is a guess, not a finding.
Incorrect. This guesses at a cause without supporting data.
Correct. This describes behavior, quotes the client, and states the objective finding.
Incorrect. This is vague and gives no findings the next nurse can use.
questions.rationale: Objective documentation describes what the nurse saw and heard and quotes the client, without labels or guesses about cause. The best entry records the behavior, the client’s exact words, and orientation, which shows a clear change from admission. The withdrawal entry is tempting because it offers an explanation, but guessing at diagnoses in the record is inappropriate without data. Labels like “combative” tell the next nurse less than a description does.
questions.takeaway: Chart behaviors and quotes, not labels or guesses about cause.
questions.hintContent: Which entry would let a stranger picture exactly what happened?
questions.hintStrategy: For “best entry” items, choose the one with times, quotes, and observable findings; reject labels and speculation.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client’s blood pressure drops after surgery, and the nurse calls the provider. Which entry best documents this communication?
options: “1520: Dr. Lee told of BP 84/50, HR 118; bolus ordered, read back. 1550: BP 102/64.”
“1520: Provider aware of low blood pressure; will continue to monitor closely.”
“1520: Notified provider of change in condition. Client appears stable at this time.”
“1520: Dr. Lee called about BP 84/50 and HR 118; orders received.”
optionRationales: Correct. This includes time, clinician, findings, response, and outcome.
Incorrect. “Provider aware” does not show what was reported or what the plan was.
Incorrect. This is vague and lacks findings, orders, and outcome.
Incorrect. This entry names the provider and the findings, but it omits what was ordered, the read-back, and the client’s response, so the story is incomplete.
questions.rationale: A complete notification entry names who was told, when, what findings were reported, the response or orders, and what happened next. “Provider aware” is incomplete because the reader cannot tell what was reported or what was decided. The entry that names Dr. Lee and the vital signs is tempting because it is specific, but it leaves out the orders, the read-back, and the client’s response. The best note tells a clear care story another nurse could act on.
questions.takeaway: Notification entries need who, when, what was reported, the response, and the outcome.
questions.hintContent: Look for the entry that tells the whole story from finding to result.
questions.hintStrategy: For documentation-quality items, choose the entry that a stranger could act on without asking questions.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is about to leave for a meal break. A coworker who is still logged in at a shared workstation says, “Just chart your 1200 vitals under my login. It saves time.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Okay, but I’ll add my initials in the note so everyone knows.”
“Thanks. I’ll do it now and log you out when I’m done.”
“I’ll write them down and chart them after my break.”
“No thanks. I’ll log out your session and sign in as myself.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Adding initials does not fix charting under another person’s identity.
Incorrect. Using another person’s login misattributes the entry and breaks accountability.
Incorrect. Avoiding the coworker’s login is right, but the open session is left unsecured and charting is delayed when the nurse could sign in now.
Correct. Each nurse charts under their own credentials, and the open session is secured.
questions.rationale: Use only your own login and never chart under a colleague’s session. The audit trail records who entered information, so charting under another person’s login falsely attributes the entry and breaks accountability. Adding initials in the note is tempting because it seems to identify the true author, but the system still records the wrong user. The nurse secures the coworker’s open session and signs in under their own credentials.
questions.takeaway: Chart only under your own login; secure any session left open by someone else.
questions.hintContent: Whose name will the audit trail attach to the entry?
questions.hintStrategy: For EHR access items, reject any shortcut that uses another person’s credentials.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse preceptor reviews a new graduate’s entries for the morning, shown in the exhibit. It is now 1030. Which entry should the preceptor address first?

rows: Client pleasant and cooperative with care.
Client c/o nausea; antiemetic given per order.
Metoprolol 25 mg PO given; tolerated well.

options: The 0800 entry describing the client as pleasant.
The 1100 entry documenting metoprolol as given.
The 0930 entry using the abbreviation “c/o.”
The 1000 entry stating that the provider is aware.
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is vague but does not misrepresent care.
Correct. This charts a medication not yet given, a false record that could cause a missed or double dose.
Incorrect. Abbreviation use follows policy and is a minor issue.
Incorrect. This is incomplete and needs detail, but it is less dangerous than a false medication record.
questions.rationale: All four entries could be improved, but the precharted medication is the most serious because it creates a false record of care. Another nurse may believe the dose was given and skip it, or the dose may be given twice. “Provider aware” is the most tempting choice because it is a well-known incomplete entry, but it does not directly misstate whether care occurred. Prioritize the entry with the greatest risk of client harm.
questions.takeaway: A precharted medication is a false record and the highest-risk documentation error.
questions.hintContent: Compare the time on each entry with the current time.
questions.hintStrategy: When several entries are flawed, prioritize the one that could directly cause client harm.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: While walking through the hospital cafeteria, a nurse finds a printed unit census sheet with client names, room numbers, and diagnoses left on a table. What should the nurse do first?
options: Pick up the sheet so no one else can read it.
Report the finding to the privacy officer from the unit.
Ask nearby staff who left the sheet on the table.
Leave it in place and call the charge nurse to retrieve it.
optionRationales: Correct. Securing the exposed information stops further disclosure.
Incorrect. Reporting is required but comes after securing the information.
Incorrect. Finding the person can wait until the information is protected.
Incorrect. Leaving it exposed allows more people to see it.
questions.rationale: When an exposed record is found, the nurse secures it first and then follows reporting policy. Picking up the sheet immediately stops additional people from viewing protected health information. Reporting to the privacy officer is tempting because breaches must be reported, but the exposure continues while the sheet sits on the table. Afterward, the nurse reports the incident and disposes of the sheet through approved methods.
questions.takeaway: Secure exposed health information first, then report per policy.
questions.hintContent: Which action stops the exposure right now?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy breaches, “first” usually means containing the exposure before reporting.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 1400, a nurse charts, “New irregular pulse 118/min, client reports palpitations and lightheadedness.” The nurse plans to let the provider review the note during evening rounds at 1700. What should the charge nurse tell the nurse?
options: “Good thinking. A detailed note saves time during rounds.”
“Add a flag to the note so the provider sees it first.”
“Call the provider now to report this change directly.”
“Recheck the pulse at 1700 before rounds and then decide.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A note does not reach the provider in time for a new, possibly unstable change.
Incorrect. A flag still depends on someone reading the record later.
Correct. A new change with symptoms needs direct communication now; the record does not replace it.
Incorrect. Waiting three hours delays evaluation of a symptomatic new rhythm.
questions.rationale: Documentation never replaces direct communication. A new irregular, fast pulse with palpitations and lightheadedness may signal an unstable rhythm and needs prompt, direct reporting to the provider. Adding a flag is tempting because it seems to highlight the problem, but it still depends on someone reading the chart later. After reporting, the nurse documents who was told, when, the response, and the plan.
questions.takeaway: A significant new finding is reported directly; charting it is not enough.
questions.hintContent: How quickly will the provider learn about the change in each option?
questions.hintStrategy: If a finding is new and symptomatic, choose direct, immediate communication over record-based options.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client is on postoperative day 2 of a hip replacement critical pathway. The plan calls for walking in the hallway three times today. During the first walk, the client becomes pale and says, “I feel like I’m going to pass out.” What should the nurse do first?

rows: Pain 3/10 or less on oral meds

options: Document a variance from the pathway in the record.
Walk the client back to the room quickly to lie down.
Notify the case manager that discharge may be delayed.
Have the client sit or lie down and check vital signs.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Documentation follows the client’s safety.
Incorrect. Getting the client to lie down is right, but walking further while near-fainting risks a fall; the nurse should sit or lower the client where they are.
Incorrect. This is not the immediate need while the client feels faint.
Correct. Preventing a fall and assessing the cause come first.
questions.rationale: A critical pathway lists expected care and outcomes, but the client always comes before the template. The client is near-fainting, so the nurse has the client sit or lie down right away to prevent a fall and checks vital signs before anything else. Walking the client back to the room delays this and risks a fall. Documenting the variance is tempting because the stem highlights the pathway, but variance charting, with actions and the client’s response, comes after the client is safe.
questions.takeaway: When a client deviates from a pathway, ensure safety first, then document the variance and response.
questions.hintContent: The exhibit is about the plan; the client is about to faint.
questions.hintStrategy: When exhibit data and client symptoms compete, act on the symptoms first.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A client is going home today after starting enoxaparin injections. During return demonstration, the client cannot remember where to inject and drops the syringe. The discharge note from the prior shift reads, “Teaching complete; client verbalizes understanding.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Reteach the injection steps and have the client demonstrate again.
Notify the provider that discharge may need to be delayed.
Add a home health referral to the note and discharge the client as planned.
Give the client a printed guide with pictures of each step.
optionRationales: Correct. The real learning gap must be addressed before the client goes home.
Incorrect. Discharge may change if the client still cannot inject, but it is too early to decide that before reteaching and rechecking.
Incorrect. Referral may help, but the client must be safe with injections at discharge.
Incorrect. A picture guide is a helpful support, but it does not show the client can do the skill; a return demonstration is needed first.
questions.rationale: Transition notes must reflect real learning and every unresolved need, and a printed packet or “verbalizes understanding” does not prove it. The client’s failed demonstration shows a learning gap that matters for safety, so the nurse reteaches and has the client try again. Then the nurse documents the actual result, remaining needs, and follow-up. Adding a home health referral is tempting, but the client may need to give an injection before the first visit.
questions.takeaway: Document real demonstrated learning and close gaps before discharge.
questions.hintContent: Does the record match what the client can actually do?
questions.hintStrategy: When documentation conflicts with what the nurse observes, trust the observation and act on it first.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a coworker on the same unit reading the chart of a well-known local athlete who is a client on a different floor. The coworker is not involved in the athlete’s care. What should the nurse do first?
options: Report the coworker to the privacy officer without speaking to her.
Ask the coworker to close the record right away.
Tell the charge nurse about it at the end of the shift.
Remind the coworker that audits track every chart opened.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting may follow, but the ongoing access should be stopped first.
Correct. This stops the unauthorized access now.
Incorrect. The charge nurse should be told, but waiting until the end of the shift lets the access continue now.
Incorrect. Mentioning audits may discourage her, but it does not directly stop the access; the nurse should ask her to close the record.
questions.rationale: Opening a record without a care-related purpose is a privacy breach, even if the person only looks. The nurse first stops the access by asking the coworker to close the record, then follows facility policy for reporting. Reporting directly to the privacy officer is tempting because policy requires reporting, but it does not stop the exposure happening now. The audit trail will show who accessed the record.
questions.takeaway: Stop unauthorized access first, then report through policy.
questions.hintContent: Which option ends the breach that is happening now?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy “first” items, contain the breach before reporting.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with an abdominal incision reports pain. Which entry best documents the pain assessment?
options: “Client appears to be in a great deal of pain and is very uncomfortable.”
“Client reports pain 6/10; analgesic given per order.”
“Client states, ‘It burns, 6 out of 10.’ Guarding incision; HR 98.”
“Client states pain is bad; resting in bed with eyes closed.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is a vague impression with no client report or findings.
Incorrect. The rating and action are useful, but the entry lacks the client’s description and objective findings, so the assessment is incomplete.
Correct. This quotes the client’s report and adds objective findings.
Incorrect. Quoting the client is good, but “bad” has no rating, and the observation does not describe the pain.
questions.rationale: Record pain as the client reports it, using the client’s words, plus observable findings. A quote preserves meaning, and guarding and heart rate add objective data. A rating with the action taken is tempting because it is accurate, but it leaves out the quality of the pain and objective findings. Vague words like “bad” or opinions about how much pain the client “appears” to have tell the next nurse little.
questions.takeaway: Chart pain as the client’s quoted report plus objective findings.
questions.hintContent: Which entry gives both the client’s words and what the nurse observed?
questions.hintStrategy: For subjective-data entries, choose the quote plus objective findings.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A unit uses focus charting with Data, Action, and Response (DAR). A nurse writes a note with the focus “Acute pain.” Which statement belongs in the Response section?
options: “1130: Client rates pain 2/10 and is resting with eyes closed.”
“1100: Client rates incision pain 8/10 and is guarding.”
“1100: Oxycodone 5 mg PO given per order; repositioned.”
“Plan: reassess the client’s pain level every 2 hours and as needed.”
optionRationales: Correct. Response is the client’s outcome after the action.
Incorrect. This is Data: assessment findings that prompted the action.
Incorrect. This is Action: what the nurse did.
Incorrect. This is a plan, not the client’s response.
questions.rationale: Focus charting centers on one concern and commonly uses Data, Action, and Response. Data records the findings, Action records what the nurse did, and Response records how the client responded. The reassessment showing pain 2/10 is the Response. The plan to reassess is tempting because it follows the action, but it states future care rather than the client’s outcome.
questions.takeaway: In DAR notes, Response is the client’s measured outcome after the action.
questions.hintContent: Ask which statement shows what happened to the client after care.
questions.hintStrategy: For charting-format items, map each option to a section before choosing.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client is being transferred from a community hospital to a regional ICU. The receiving ICU nurse asks for the client’s current medications, allergies, recent labs, and relevant history. Which action by the sending nurse is correct?
options: Share only the diagnosis because of the minimum-necessary rule.
Ask the client to sign a release before sharing anything.
Have the provider call the ICU provider to share the information.
Send the requested treatment information through approved channels.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Minimum necessary does not limit sharing for treatment between providers.
Incorrect. Sharing between providers for treatment does not require a separate release.
Incorrect. Provider-to-provider talk is valuable, but the nurses still need a direct handoff, and the sending nurse can share this information.
Correct. Providers may share information needed for treatment using approved systems.
questions.rationale: HIPAA’s minimum-necessary rule limits sharing to what is needed, but it does not apply to disclosures between providers for treatment. The receiving team needs current status, medications, allergies, labs, and history for safe continuity, sent through approved channels. Limiting the report to the diagnosis is tempting because it sounds protective, but it would leave the ICU team without information needed to keep the client safe. Privacy rules have specific exceptions, so neither “always share” nor “never share” is correct.
questions.takeaway: The minimum-necessary rule does not block sharing among providers for treatment.
questions.hintContent: What is the purpose of this disclosure?
questions.hintStrategy: For privacy items, identify the purpose first: treatment sharing among providers is allowed through approved channels.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse reviewing a medical-surgical chart sees that the client’s daughter told the admitting nurse that her mother “walks independently with a cane at home.” The nurse has not yet seen the client walk. Which entry is most accurate?
options: “Ambulates independently with a cane; gait steady and even.”
“Daughter reports client uses a cane at home; gait not yet assessed.”
“Client walks well with a cane per family; no fall risk noted.”
“Gait steady; independent with a cane per the admission note.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This charts an observed finding the nurse has not assessed.
Correct. This attributes the report and states what has not been observed.
Incorrect. This draws a conclusion from unverified data.
Incorrect. This copies an unverified finding as if it were current.
questions.rationale: Separate your own assessment from another person’s report, and attribute reports to their source. The daughter’s statement is useful history, but it is not an observed gait assessment, and the entry should say so. Copying the admission note is tempting because it seems efficient, but carrying forward a finding the nurse did not verify can mislead the team about fall risk. The accurate entry is honest about what was and was not assessed.
questions.takeaway: Attribute reported information to its source and never chart it as your own observation.
questions.hintContent: Who actually observed the client walking?
questions.hintStrategy: For attribution items, choose the entry that names the source and states what the nurse did not verify.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A client refuses a prescribed subcutaneous heparin injection, saying, “I bruise too easily from those shots.” After teaching, the client still declines. Which information should the nurse document? Select all that apply.
options: The dose marked as given so the MAR stays complete.
The nurse’s view that the client is being stubborn.
The client’s stated reason, quoted in the client’s words.
The teaching given about the purpose and risks of refusing.
The time the provider was notified and the response.
“Client noncompliant with anticoagulant therapy.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Charting a refused dose as given is falsification.
Incorrect. Personal opinions about motive do not belong in the record.
Correct. Quoting the reason preserves the meaning of the choice.
Correct. This shows the client made an informed decision.
Correct. Notification with the response completes the care story.
Incorrect. “Noncompliant” is a label without useful detail.
questions.rationale: When a client declines care, the record should show the decision, the stated reason, the teaching given, and notification and follow-up. Quoting the client keeps the meaning and avoids judgment. “Noncompliant” is tempting because it is a familiar term, but it is a label that tells the next nurse nothing about why or what was done. Marking a refused dose as given would be a false record.
questions.takeaway: Document a refusal with the quote, teaching, notification, and follow-up, not a label.
questions.hintContent: Which items would let the next nurse understand the refusal fully?
questions.hintStrategy: For documentation SATA items, select facts, quotes, and actions; reject labels, opinions, and anything false.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse educator asks new graduates to identify objective, well-written entries. Which entries meet this standard? Select all that apply.
options: “1100: Turned away and said, ‘Leave me alone,’ when PT arrived.”
“1300: Client lazy about walking; refused hallway walk.”
“1400: Right ankle edema, 2+ pitting, warm to touch.”
“1500: Client doing well and in good spirits.”
“0930: Ate 25% of breakfast; stated, ‘My stomach feels full.’”
“1015: Client hostile toward staff during bath.”
optionRationales: Correct. It describes observed behavior and quotes the client.
Incorrect. “Lazy” is judgmental and guesses at motive.
Correct. It describes specific, measurable findings.
Incorrect. This is vague and gives no measurable findings.
Correct. It records a measured amount and quotes the client.
Incorrect. “Hostile” is a label, not a description of behavior.
questions.rationale: Objective documentation describes specific findings the nurse can see, hear, measure, or feel, written without judgment. Measured intake, quoted statements, described behavior, and graded edema all meet this standard. “Doing well and in good spirits” is tempting because it is positive and not judgmental, but it is vague and gives the next nurse nothing to compare. Labels such as “hostile” or “lazy” guess at motive.
questions.takeaway: Objective entries use measurements, descriptions, and quotes; avoid labels and vague summaries.
questions.hintContent: Could another nurse verify or compare each entry later?
questions.hintStrategy: For “which entries are objective” items, select those with measurable or quoted content.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A charge nurse observes staff during a shift. Which actions are breaches of client confidentiality that require follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Two nurses discuss a client’s diagnosis by name in a crowded elevator.
A nurse leaves a client’s record open on an unlocked screen.
A nurse shares wound findings with the client’s physical therapist.
A nurse looks up a coworker’s lab results out of concern.
A nurse verifies a caller with the client’s code before sharing updates.
optionRationales: Correct. Public discussion exposes health information to others.
Correct. An unlocked screen allows unauthorized viewing.
Incorrect. Sharing with the treating team for care is appropriate.
Correct. Accessing a record without a care role is a breach.
Incorrect. Verifying identity per policy protects privacy.
questions.rationale: Use and share records only for an authorized role and purpose. Discussing clients in public spaces, leaving screens unlocked, and viewing records without a care need all breach confidentiality. Looking up a coworker’s results is tempting to excuse because the motive is concern, but good intentions do not create authorized access. Sharing needed findings with the treating team and verifying callers per policy are appropriate.
questions.takeaway: Confidentiality means role-based access, secure screens, and private conversations.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each action has a care purpose and an authorized role.
questions.hintStrategy: For breach SATA items, judge each action by purpose and setting, not by the person’s intentions.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is oriented to a unit that uses charting by exception (CBE). Which actions by the nurse are consistent with this system? Select all that apply.
options: Skip all routine findings because normal is assumed.
Document a new finding that differs from the standard in detail.
Chart only events that need a rapid response call.
Include the actions taken and the client’s response for exceptions.
Record routine vital signs on the required flow sheet.
Review the unit’s written standards for what is considered normal.
optionRationales: Incorrect. CBE does not mean charting nothing routine.
Correct. Changes from the norm are the exceptions that must be described.
Incorrect. CBE is not “chart emergencies only.”
Correct. Exceptions need the full care story.
Correct. CBE still requires routine data in set flow sheets.
Correct. CBE depends on clearly defined norms.
questions.rationale: Charting by exception documents changes from defined standards and depends on clear norms and required flow sheets. Routine data are still recorded in their set places, and any exception is described in detail with the actions taken and the client’s response. “Normal is assumed” is the most tempting misunderstanding because it sounds like the definition, but CBE does not eliminate routine records. CBE never means charting only emergencies.
questions.takeaway: CBE = defined norms plus required flow sheets plus detailed exceptions.
questions.hintContent: What does “exception” mean if there is no defined normal?
questions.hintStrategy: For charting-system SATA items, reject any option that claims the system lets you skip required documentation.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 2100, a nurse remembers that she repositioned a client and assessed the client’s sacral skin at 1600 but did not document it. Which elements should the late entry include? Select all that apply.
options: The current date and time when the entry is written.
The time the care and assessment took place.
Placement in the 1600 slot with no mention of delay.
A note that the nurse told the oncoming shift instead.
A clear label identifying it as a late entry.
optionRationales: Correct. This shows when documentation actually occurred.
Correct. This shows when the event happened.
Incorrect. This backdates the entry and hides the delay.
Incorrect. Verbal report does not replace the written entry.
Correct. The label makes the timing transparent.
questions.rationale: A late entry is an addition made after the event and is clearly labeled with both the entry time and the event time, per policy. This keeps the record accurate and transparent. Placing the note in the 1600 slot is tempting because the care did happen then, but it hides when the documentation was written. Verbal handoff is important but does not replace documentation.
questions.takeaway: Late entries are labeled and show both when written and when care occurred.
questions.hintContent: An honest record shows both times.
questions.hintStrategy: For late-entry SATA items, select transparency about timing; reject backdating.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 0310, a nurse finds a client on the floor. After assessment, help to bed, and notification of the provider, the nurse documents the event. Which items belong in the client’s record? Select all that apply.
options: The provider notified, the time, and orders received.
“Client fell because she ignored instructions to call for help.”
The nurse’s opinion that low staffing caused the fall.
The time the client was found and the position found in.
The client’s own words about what happened.
Assessment findings, including any injury.
optionRationales: Correct. This documents communication and the plan.
Incorrect. This assigns blame and guesses at cause.
Incorrect. Speculation and blame do not belong in the clinical record.
Correct. Time and objective description start the care story.
Correct. A quote preserves the client’s account.
Correct. Findings show the client’s condition after the fall.
questions.rationale: A fall note should tell a factual care story: when and how the client was found, the client’s own account, assessment findings, notification, orders, and the client’s response. Blaming the client is tempting because it may explain what happened, but it guesses at motive and is not objective. Opinions about staffing are not clinical findings. Describe facts, attribute statements, and avoid blame.
questions.takeaway: Document a fall with facts, quotes, findings, and notification, not blame or opinion.
questions.hintContent: Which items could another nurse verify or act on?
questions.hintStrategy: For “what belongs in the record” SATA items, select objective facts and actions; reject blame and speculation.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: After a telephone call to report a change in a client’s condition, a nurse documents the communication. Which elements are needed for a complete entry? Select all that apply.
options: A brief note that says only “provider aware.”
The name of the provider who was contacted.
The time of the call.
The specific findings the nurse reported.
The provider’s response and any orders received.
optionRationales: Incorrect. This omits what was reported and what was decided.
Correct. The reader needs to know who received the report.
Correct. Timing shows how quickly the change was reported.
Correct. This shows what information the provider had.
Correct. This shows the plan that resulted.
questions.rationale: “Provider aware” is incomplete. A complete communication entry names who was contacted, when, what findings were reported, the response or orders, and what happened next. This lets the next nurse continue the plan and supports accountability. The short note is tempting because it is quick and familiar, but it leaves the reader guessing about the content and outcome of the call.
questions.takeaway: Document who, when, what was reported, and the response for every provider notification.
questions.hintContent: Could the next nurse continue the plan from this entry alone?
questions.hintStrategy: For complete-entry SATA items, select every element that answers who, when, what, and what next.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nursing student is assigned to a client on a medical unit for clinical practice. Which actions by the student are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Print the client’s history to finish the care plan at home.
Look up a relative’s chart while logged in for clinical.
Lock or log out of the workstation when stepping away.
Share the login with a classmate whose access is delayed.
Access only the assigned client’s record under supervision.
Remove names and identifiers from the care plan paperwork.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Keeping identifiable records outside approved use is not allowed.
Incorrect. Access without a care role is a breach.
Correct. This prevents unauthorized viewing.
Incorrect. Each person uses only their own credentials.
Correct. Students need supervised, authorized access tied to their role.
Correct. De-identified notes protect privacy.
questions.rationale: Students need supervised, authorized access, and “for education” does not allow browsing or keeping identifiable records. Appropriate actions include accessing only the assigned client, de-identifying paperwork, and securing the workstation. Printing the history is tempting because it supports learning, but removing identifiable records from the facility risks a breach. Sharing logins breaks accountability in the audit trail.
questions.takeaway: Students access only assigned records, de-identify notes, and never share logins.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each action is tied to the student’s authorized role.
questions.hintStrategy: For student-access SATA items, “for education” never overrides privacy rules.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
